questions.stem: What is asexual reproduction?
options: Producing offspring from two parents, by gametes fusing
Producing offspring from one parent, by two of its gametes fusing
Producing offspring by meiosis followed by fertilisation
Producing offspring from one parent, without gametes fusing
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction involves a single parent and no fusion of gametes, so the offspring are genetically identical to the parent unless a mutation occurs. Self-fertilisation still involves gametes, so it is sexual.

questions.stem: How do bacteria reproduce by binary fission?
options: A small outgrowth forms on the cell and breaks off when mature
Two bacterial cells fuse and their DNA combines to form a zygote
The cell releases many spores that are carried away by the wind
The DNA is copied and the cell splits into two identical cells
questions.explanation: In binary fission the circular chromosome is copied, the cell grows, and it divides into two genetically identical cells. An outgrowth that breaks off is budding.

questions.stem: A yeast cell forms a small outgrowth that grows and then separates to become a new cell. Which type of asexual reproduction is this?
options: Spore formation
Vegetative propagation
Budding
Binary fission
questions.explanation: In budding a new individual grows as an outgrowth of the parent and then separates, as in yeast and hydra. In binary fission the parent cell divides into two cells of about equal size.

questions.stem: Strawberry plants send out runners that take root and grow into new plants. What type of reproduction is this?
options: Vegetative propagation
Spore formation
Binary fission
Cross-pollination by insects
questions.explanation: Vegetative propagation produces new plants from parts of the parent such as runners, tubers or bulbs, without seeds. The new plants are genetically identical to the parent.

questions.stem: Which organism commonly reproduces asexually by forming spores?
options: Yeast, by forming outgrowths
A bacterium, by splitting in two
Bread mould, a type of fungus
A potato plant, from its tubers
questions.explanation: Bread mould produces huge numbers of tiny spores that disperse through the air and grow into new moulds. Potatoes use vegetative propagation, yeast buds, and bacteria divide by binary fission.

questions.stem: Which list correctly matches organisms to their method of asexual reproduction?
options: Bacterium: tubers. Hydra: spores. Potato: binary fission
Bacterium: binary fission. Hydra: budding. Potato: tubers
Bacterium: budding. Hydra: tubers. Potato: binary fission
Bacterium: spores. Hydra: binary fission. Potato: budding
questions.explanation: Bacteria divide by binary fission, hydra grow buds that break away, and potatoes form underground stem tubers that grow into new plants, a form of vegetative propagation.

questions.stem: A bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes in ideal conditions. Starting with one cell, how many cells will there be after 2 hours?
questions.explanation: Two hours is 6 periods of 20 minutes, and the number doubles each period: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 64. Thirty-two would be after only 5 divisions.

questions.stem: A gardener takes cuttings from a grapevine that produces excellent fruit and grows them into new vines. Why do the new vines produce the same fruit?
options: They developed the same fruit because they were grown in the same soil
They are genetically identical to the parent vine, as they were produced by mitosis
They received half of their alleles from the parent vine and half from another vine
They inherited the parent's fruit quality through gametes formed by meiosis
questions.explanation: Cuttings grow by mitosis, so the new vines are clones with the same alleles as the parent. Gametes and meiosis are part of sexual reproduction, which would mix alleles.

questions.stem: Which is a biological advantage of asexual reproduction?
options: Offspring have new combinations of alleles from two parents
A single parent can produce many offspring quickly without a mate
Offspring are genetically varied and can survive many diseases
Offspring are always much better adapted than their single parent
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction needs no mate and is usually fast, so a well-suited organism can rapidly colonise an area. Genetic variation and new allele combinations come from sexual reproduction.

questions.stem: Which is a biological disadvantage of asexual reproduction?
options: Offspring are genetically different from the parent, losing useful traits
Offspring lack genetic variation, so a change in conditions could kill them all
It needs two parents to meet, which wastes time and energy finding a mate
It produces very few offspring, so the populations grow very slowly
questions.explanation: Clones share the same alleles, so a new disease or environmental change that harms one is likely to harm all of them. Asexual reproduction usually produces many offspring quickly and needs only one parent.

questions.stem: Aphids reproduce asexually through summer, when food is plentiful, and switch to sexual reproduction in autumn. Which explanation best fits this pattern?
options: Asexual reproduction gives variation in summer; sexual reproduction makes identical offspring to survive winter
Sexual reproduction is faster, so it is used when the aphids have little time left before winter
Asexual reproduction needs low temperatures, so it can only happen in summer when the aphids are active
Asexual reproduction rapidly exploits stable good conditions; sexual reproduction gives variation before conditions change
questions.explanation: When conditions are stable and favourable, fast cloning builds numbers. Before conditions change, sexual reproduction produces varied offspring, some of which may cope better with the new conditions.

questions.stem: Bananas grown commercially are almost all one variety propagated by cuttings. Why does a new fungal disease pose a serious threat to them?
options: The plants have many different alleles, so the fungus can attack each one
The plants produce spores, which carry the fungus to new areas very quickly
The plants are genetically identical, so if one is susceptible they all are
The plants reproduce sexually, so the disease spreads in their pollen
questions.explanation: Propagation by cuttings produces clones with no genetic variation, so none are likely to carry resistance and the whole crop is at risk. Genetic diversity is what gives some individuals a chance of resisting a disease.

questions.stem: Compared with asexual reproduction, what is the main biological advantage of reproducing sexually?
options: It produces offspring identical to the parents
It produces genetically diverse offspring
It produces offspring more quickly
It needs only one parent to reproduce
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction combines alleles from two parents in new ways, so offspring differ from each other and from their parents. This diversity makes it more likely some will survive a change in the environment.

questions.stem: In humans, which type of cell division produces gametes?
options: Meiosis
Mitosis
Binary fission
Budding
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, producing haploid sperm or eggs with 23 chromosomes each. Mitosis produces body cells with the full 46 chromosomes.

questions.stem: How many chromosomes are in a human sperm cell?
questions.explanation: Gametes are haploid: they contain one chromosome from each of the 23 pairs. Body cells are diploid with 46 chromosomes.

questions.stem: Why must gametes contain half the normal number of chromosomes?
options: So that the offspring receive all their chromosomes from one parent
So that the zygote can divide by meiosis immediately after fertilisation
So that fertilisation restores the full number of chromosomes in the zygote
So that the gametes are small enough to move very quickly towards the egg
questions.explanation: When two haploid gametes fuse, the zygote has the full diploid number, 23 + 23 = 46 in humans. Without halving, the chromosome number would double every generation.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the roles of mitosis and meiosis in a human life cycle?
options: Mitosis makes gametes; after fertilisation, meiosis grows the zygote into a body
Meiosis makes body cells for growth; mitosis makes gametes for reproduction
Mitosis and meiosis both make gametes, but only in different organs
Meiosis makes gametes; after fertilisation, mitosis grows the zygote into a body
questions.explanation: Meiosis in the testes and ovaries produces haploid gametes. After fertilisation, the diploid zygote divides repeatedly by mitosis to form all the cells of the body.

questions.stem: Which comparison of mitosis and meiosis is correct?
options: Mitosis gives 2 varied haploid cells; meiosis gives 4 identical diploid cells
Mitosis gives 4 identical diploid cells; meiosis gives 2 varied haploid cells
Mitosis gives 2 identical diploid cells; meiosis gives 4 varied haploid cells
Mitosis gives 4 varied haploid cells; meiosis gives 2 identical diploid cells
questions.explanation: Mitosis is one division producing two cells genetically identical to the parent. Meiosis is two divisions producing four haploid cells that are genetically different from each other.

questions.stem: What must happen to the genetic material before a cell divides by mitosis or binary fission?
options: It must be halved so that each new cell gets half a set
It must be mixed with the DNA from another cell of the species
It must be broken down so that new DNA can be made later
It must be copied so that each new cell gets a complete set
questions.explanation: The DNA is replicated before division, so each daughter cell receives a full, identical copy of the genetic material. This is how genetic information passes from one cell generation to the next.

questions.stem: Brothers and sisters with the same two parents (who are not identical twins) differ genetically. Which process contributes to this?
options: Each child receives all of its chromosomes from only one of its two parents
Each child's DNA is changed by the environment during its early development
Each gamete receives a random mix of chromosomes from each pair during meiosis
Each body cell is made by mitosis, which mixes chromosomes from both parents
questions.explanation: In meiosis the members of each chromosome pair are shared out to gametes independently and randomly, so each gamete carries a different combination. Mitosis produces identical copies and does not mix chromosomes.

questions.stem: What is crossing over?
options: Movement of whole chromosomes between two cells during mitosis
Fusion of a sperm and an egg to form a single zygote
Copying of all the DNA before a cell divides in two
Exchange of sections between paired chromosomes during meiosis
questions.explanation: During meiosis, paired chromosomes from the two parents exchange sections, producing chromosomes with new combinations of alleles. This adds to the variation among gametes.

questions.stem: Why does random fertilisation increase genetic variation among offspring?
options: Only the fittest sperm can fertilise an egg, so offspring are always improved
Fertilisation causes new mutations in the chromosomes of the zygote
Fertilisation doubles the chromosome number of the zygote each generation
Any one of many different sperm can fuse with any one of many different eggs
questions.explanation: Each parent produces gametes with many different combinations of alleles, and which sperm meets which egg is a matter of chance. This multiplies the number of possible genotypes in offspring.

questions.stem: Which combination of processes gives an offspring from two parents its unique genetic identity?
options: Mitosis in the zygote, then meiosis in each of its body cells
Crossing over and random assortment in meiosis, then random fertilisation
Replication of DNA and division by mitosis, then binary fission
Budding and vegetative propagation, then spore formation
questions.explanation: Crossing over and the random sharing of chromosome pairs in meiosis make each gamete different, and random fertilisation combines two of these gametes. Mitosis, budding and fission produce identical copies.

questions.stem: Identical twins have the same DNA, while non-identical twins share only about half their alleles on average. Which explains the difference?
options: Identical twins come from one parent only; non-identical twins come from two separate sets of parents
Identical twins come from one zygote that splits; non-identical twins come from two eggs and two sperm
Identical twins come from two eggs and one sperm; non-identical twins come from one egg and two sperm
Identical twins come from mitosis in an egg; non-identical twins come from meiosis in a zygote
questions.explanation: Identical twins form when one zygote divides into two embryos by mitosis, so they share the same genome. Non-identical twins come from two separate eggs, each fertilised by a different sperm, so they are as different as ordinary siblings.

questions.stem: What is a zygote?
options: An embryo that has implanted in the uterus lining
A bud that has broken away from the body of a parent hydra
The diploid cell formed when a sperm and an egg fuse
A haploid cell formed by meiosis in the ovary
questions.explanation: Fertilisation produces a single diploid cell, the zygote, which divides by mitosis to form the embryo. Haploid cells formed by meiosis are gametes.

questions.stem: Why does a bread mould release enormous numbers of spores?
options: Each spore must fuse with another spore before it can grow into a new mould
Each spore carries only part of the mould's DNA, so many must combine
Spores are produced only by meiosis, so many are needed to give variation
Most spores land where they cannot grow, so many are needed for a few to succeed
questions.explanation: Spores are dispersed at random by air, and most land in unsuitable places, so producing vast numbers makes it likely some reach food. Asexual spores grow into new moulds on their own without fusing.

questions.stem: Where are sperm produced in the human male?
options: In the sperm duct
In the testes
In the prostate gland
In the urethra
questions.explanation: Sperm are made by meiosis in the testes, which also produce testosterone. The sperm duct and urethra carry sperm, and the prostate gland adds fluid.

questions.stem: What is the function of the ovaries?
options: Producing the fluid that nourishes and carries the male sperm
Producing eggs and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone
Providing the place where an embryo implants and develops
Carrying eggs from the uterus to the outside of the body
questions.explanation: The ovaries produce eggs and secrete oestrogen and progesterone. The embryo implants in the uterus lining.

questions.stem: Where in the female reproductive system does fertilisation normally take place?
options: In the oviduct (fallopian tube)
In the ovary, before ovulation
In the cervix, just below the uterus
In the lining of the uterus
questions.explanation: After ovulation, the egg moves into the oviduct, where it may meet sperm and be fertilised. The zygote then divides as it moves to the uterus, where the embryo implants.

questions.stem: What is the role of the uterus?
options: It is where sperm are stored before they mature
It is where the egg is usually fertilised by a sperm
It is where the embryo implants and develops into a fetus
It is where eggs are produced by meiosis each month
questions.explanation: The uterus has a thick, blood-rich lining in which the embryo implants, and its muscular wall stretches as the fetus grows and contracts at birth. Eggs are made in the ovaries and usually fertilised in the oviduct.

questions.stem: What is the role of the fluids added by the prostate gland and seminal vesicles?
options: They produce testosterone, which controls the development of the male body
They carry the sperm and provide nutrients that the sperm use for energy
They produce sperm by meiosis before the sperm enter the testes
They store the sperm until they are fully mature and able to swim well
questions.explanation: These glands add fluid to sperm to form semen, which carries the sperm and supplies sugar for energy. Sperm are made in the testes, which also produce testosterone.

questions.stem: A man has a blockage in both sperm ducts (vas deferens). Which outcome is expected?
options: No sperm are made because the testes stop working
Testosterone can no longer reach the rest of the body
Semen can no longer be produced by the prostate gland at all
Sperm are still made but cannot leave the body in semen
questions.explanation: The sperm ducts carry sperm from the testes towards the urethra. If they are blocked, sperm cannot reach the semen, although the testes still make sperm and testosterone, which travels in the blood.

questions.stem: Why is the human egg much larger than a sperm cell?
options: It contains stored food for the early embryo
It contains twice as many chromosomes as a sperm
It has to swim much further than the sperm
It contains many mitochondria to power its tail
questions.explanation: The egg's cytoplasm holds nutrients that support the zygote's first divisions. Egg and sperm each have 23 chromosomes, and it is the sperm, not the egg, that has a tail and swims.

questions.stem: How is a sperm cell adapted to reach and fertilise an egg?
options: A tail for swimming, many mitochondria and enzymes in its head
A large store of food in its cytoplasm and a thick protective coat
Two complete sets of chromosomes and a large central vacuole
A cell wall for protection and chloroplasts to supply energy
questions.explanation: The tail moves the sperm, mitochondria in the midpiece supply ATP for swimming, and enzymes in the head help it penetrate the outer layers of the egg. The sperm is haploid, with one set of chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which process links the human reproductive system to the continuity of life across generations?
options: Binary fission in the gonads makes gametes, which divide by budding to form an embryo
Meiosis in the uterus makes body cells, which grow into the embryo by fertilisation
Meiosis in the gonads makes haploid gametes, which fuse to form a diploid zygote
Mitosis in the gonads makes diploid gametes, which fuse to form a tetraploid zygote
questions.explanation: Gametes made by meiosis in the testes and ovaries carry one set of chromosomes each; fertilisation restores the diploid number and passes genetic material from both parents to the next generation.
